demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson's answers, in steps 3 and 6, must come from the kit's own rows, where the worker writes the note it traces, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: Direct reads: the records the push left, and the answer through the API
demos.purpose: Firestore read directly with your own credentials, then the API's two doors onto the same records: the ledger it serves and the question it answers. The push ended in writes, and two keys find them all without a search, as lesson 1.4 showed. The ledger row is named after the object, sources/acme~pubsub_trace_note.md, and it names the version's key, doc_key. The cell reads the ledger row, the claim, the version's chunk rows and acme's ledger summary, and holds each generation against the object's: Three generations, one number: the object's, the ledger's and the claim's. That equality is the trace's proof that one notice, delivered and acknowledged, produced every record. The chunk rows are the three the worker's chunker cuts from the note by its two rules, a chunk for each ## section and a preamble for the text above the first heading: preamble, NG-01, NG-02. This page ran the worker's own _chunk() on the note when it was built, and it cut the same three. Last, the API's two doors onto the same records. demos.heading: The burst: thirty-one objects against five instances
demos.purpose: Why squeeze. A bus that pushes has to learn how fast its reader can go, and it learns only from the answers. Pub/Sub starts a subscription's push window small, widens it with each success and narrows it with each failure (Google's push page). Cloud Run holds a request that finds no free instance in its pending queue and then refuses it with a 429. The subscription counts each refusal as a failed delivery, retries it after the backoff, and charges it against the 12 attempts; the comment in step 4's subscription is the kit's record of a first live load that learned this the hard way. At 30 in flight, 31 messages are 2 rounds of work; at 5 they are at least 7, and they have to queue. Squeezing the ceiling makes the reader the bottleneck, so you can watch the bus adapt to it. Why the corpus. make ingest-corpus uploads the kit's corpus again: by upload.sh's rule, 21 objects for acme, 3 for globex and 7 for zeta, 31 in all. Each upload is a new generation, so each fires a notice, and each notice is pushed until the worker takes it. But the bytes are the ones your lane indexed when it was built, so every claim is already taken: the worker downloads the generation, hashes it, finds the claim and answers 200 duplicate. Nothing is parsed, nothing is embedded and no model is called. The burst costs deliveries and nothing else, as long as that "every" holds, and the first cell checks it before anything moves: The ceiling is a setting of the worker's revision: the same --max-instances flag lesson-12.5.sh deploys with. Changing it deploys a new revision with the same image and the same environment. Google recommends a service-level maximum for most uses, which needs no new revision (its maximum-instances page); the revision's flag is used here so that the restore at the end puts back exactly what the kit deployed. The ceiling is a setting of the worker's revision: the same --max-instances flag lesson-12.5.sh deploys with. Changing it deploys a new revision with the same image and the same environment. Google recommends a service-level maximum for most uses, which needs no new revision (its maximum-instances page); the revision's flag is used here so that the restore at the end puts back exactly what the kit deployed. Now note the time and upload the corpus. Keep this shell open: the next three cells read BURST_SINCE. If the shell does close, export it again with the time this cell printed. Give it two minutes, then read every request Cloud Run received for the worker since BURST_SINCE, by status and by ten-second slice, with the worker's verdicts for the same window: Pub/Sub keeps its own counts for each subscription: the backlog (messages not yet acknowledged), the age of the oldest of them, and every push it made, by how the push ended. Cloud Run counts its instances the same way. These metrics are sampled every 60 seconds and can take up to 120 seconds to appear (Google's list of metrics), so run this cell at least three minutes after the upload: Put the ceiling back

demos.heading: Verify it yourself: the checklist
demos.purpose: Eight checks, each one step above, each with what a pass looks like on your lane; then the one command that puts the note away. When the checks are done, withdraw the note. make retire flags its rows as retired, with an expire_at 30 days out, marks its ledger row withdrawn, removes it from the managed stores, takes its ids out of the Vector Search index (since 13 October 2026) and moves acme's fingerprint. The object stays in the bucket, and make restore would bring it back (lesson 1.7):
